Driving Skills & Road Safety Knowledge

Braking distances, following distance, visibility, skidding, fatigue, vehicle maintenance — the practical knowledge behind safe driving.

Knowing the rules is essential — but safe driving requires understanding the physics and human factors behind those rules. Why does the stopping distance rule exist? Why does a two-second gap sometimes become a four-second gap? Why does fatigue kill as surely as alcohol?

This supplement covers the practical knowledge that the Dutch theory exam tests: the calculations, the conditions, and the decisions that determine whether a driver arrives safely.

Braking Distance

Reaction time, braking distance, stopping distance — and how speed changes everything.

The Three-Phase Stopping Process

When a driver needs to stop urgently, the vehicle covers distance in three distinct phases before it comes to rest:

  • Perception time: the time between the hazard appearing and the driver registering it — typically 0.3–0.5 seconds in alert conditions
  • Reaction time: the time between the driver recognising the hazard and their foot reaching the brake — typically 0.7–1.0 seconds in normal conditions, giving a combined perception+reaction time of about 1 second
  • Braking distance: the distance the vehicle travels from the moment the brakes are fully applied to the moment it stops completely

Stopping distance = reaction distance + braking distance. Speed dramatically increases both.

Quick Braking Distance Estimate
(speed ÷ 10) × (speed ÷ 10) = braking distance in metres
This rule of thumb applies to ideal dry conditions on a good road surface. In wet or poor conditions, multiply by 2. On ice, multiply by 10.
50 km/h
≈ 25 m braking
+ 14 m reaction
= ~39 m total
80 km/h
≈ 64 m braking
+ 22 m reaction
= ~86 m total
100 km/h
≈ 100 m braking
+ 28 m reaction
= ~128 m total
130 km/h
≈ 169 m braking
+ 36 m reaction
= ~205 m total
Speed Doubles — Distance Quadruples Critical principle

The most important physics principle for drivers: braking distance increases with the square of speed. If you double your speed, your braking distance quadruples — not doubles. Going from 50 to 100 km/h does not just double the danger; it makes the braking distance four times longer.

This is why even modest speed reductions — slowing from 130 to 100 km/h — dramatically reduce stopping distances and collision severity. A 23% reduction in speed results in a 40% reduction in stopping distance.

Factors That Increase Stopping Distance Worse conditions

The braking distances above assume ideal conditions. Many factors make stopping distances significantly longer:

  • Wet road: approximately double the dry stopping distance
  • Snow / ice: up to 10 times the dry stopping distance
  • Worn tyres: significantly reduced grip — braking distance increases substantially
  • Worn brakes: slower braking force build-up, longer distances
  • Fatigue / alcohol / medication: reaction time increases — more distance covered before braking begins
  • Downhill gradient: vehicle weight adds to stopping distance
  • Towing a trailer: heavier combination — longer stopping distance
  • Older vehicle / non-ABS brakes: less effective braking

Following Distance

The minimum safe gap between your vehicle and the one ahead — and when to increase it.

The Two-Second Rule Standard gap

The standard recommended following distance in Dutch traffic is two seconds behind the vehicle in front. To check it: when the vehicle ahead passes a fixed point (a sign, a bridge), start counting. If you reach the same point before you finish counting "one thousand and one, one thousand and two," you are too close.

Two seconds provides enough time to react and begin braking before reaching the point where the vehicle ahead is. At motorway speeds, two seconds represents a significant distance — at 120 km/h, two seconds is approximately 67 metres.

When to Increase the Gap Double or more

Two seconds is the minimum in good conditions. In any of the following circumstances, increase the gap significantly:

  • Rain or wet road: at least double — four seconds or more
  • Snow, ice or frost: ten times normal — leave enormous space
  • Fog: match your speed to your visibility — if you can see 50 metres, you must be able to stop in 50 metres
  • Towing a trailer: braking distance is longer — increase gap proportionally
  • Following a truck or bus: their stopping distance is longer and your visibility ahead is reduced — leave more space
  • Fatigue: if you feel tired, your reaction time has increased — compensate with a larger gap
  • Night driving: if you are using dipped headlights, your visibility is limited — your gap should match your braking capability within your light range
Tailgating — A Major Cause of Accidents

Following too closely — tailgating — is one of the leading causes of rear-end collisions in the Netherlands. A tailgating driver has no time to react if the vehicle ahead brakes suddenly. At 100 km/h with a one-second gap, the distance covered in reaction time alone is 28 metres — already past where the vehicle ahead was when it braked. Maintain a minimum two-second gap in all normal conditions.

Visibility & Vision

Seeing and being seen — the conditions that reduce visibility and how to respond.

The Core Visibility Principle Always applies

The RVV 1990 states it clearly: a driver must always be able to stop within the distance they can see ahead and within the distance that is clear. This is not just a rule — it is a physical safety requirement. If you cannot see further than 50 metres, you must be able to stop in 50 metres. If you cannot, you are driving too fast for the conditions.

This principle means that in fog, rain, snow or darkness, your speed may need to be far below the posted limit — because the posted limit assumes adequate visibility conditions.

🌫️ Fog

Severely reduces visibility. Use fog lights when visibility drops below 200 m (front) or 50 m (rear). Reduce speed dramatically — the posted limit does not apply when it creates a stopping distance longer than your sight line.

🌧️ Rain

Reduces visibility through the windscreen, creates spray from other vehicles, and reduces road grip simultaneously. Reduce speed, increase following distance, use headlights.

☀️ Low sun

Dawn and dusk create blinding sun angles. Use visor, sunglasses, reduce speed. Never stare at the sun — look slightly to the side of the road you are tracking.

🌙 Night driving

Dipped headlights illuminate approximately 40 metres ahead. High beams extend to 100+ metres. Match your speed to your light range. Switch to dipped headlights for oncoming traffic and when following another vehicle closely.

🚛 Following a large vehicle

A truck ahead blocks your view of the road ahead completely. Increase following distance to improve your sight line around and over the truck. Be patient — overtaking a truck requires a very long clear stretch.

↪️ Blind bends

You cannot see around a bend — neither can oncoming traffic. Reduce speed enough to stop before any hazard you might encounter. Never overtake approaching a bend. Move to the right.

Being Seen by Others Visibility both ways

Safety is not just about what you can see — it is about what others can see of you. Use lights appropriately so other drivers, cyclists and pedestrians can see you clearly:

  • Daytime running lights or dipped headlights in poor visibility, rain or dusk
  • Hazard lights when stationary on the road or approaching a major hazard
  • Warning triangle placed behind a stationary vehicle
  • High-visibility vests when exiting your vehicle on a motorway or in low-light conditions

Skidding & Loss of Control

What causes skids, how to prevent them, and what to do if one occurs.

What Causes a Skid? Grip exceeded

A skid occurs when the forces acting on a tyre exceed the available grip between that tyre and the road surface. The tyre can no longer maintain traction and slides instead of rolling. The three main causes are:

  • Braking too hard: locking the wheels causes a slide — the vehicle cannot steer when the wheels are locked
  • Accelerating too hard: the driven wheels spin instead of gripping, causing a skid on rear-wheel-drive vehicles
  • Cornering too fast: the lateral force required to follow the bend exceeds the grip, causing the vehicle to slide outward (understeer) or spin (oversteer)
Preventing Skids Always the best approach

The best response to a skid is to prevent it from happening. Key prevention techniques:

  • Brake progressively: apply brakes firmly but not so suddenly that wheels lock — ABS prevents locking on equipped vehicles
  • Reduce speed before bends: brake before the bend, not in it — braking in a corner reduces grip when you need it most for turning
  • Accelerate gently out of bends: smooth power application maintains grip
  • Increase following distance in poor conditions: less urgent braking needed
  • Check tyres regularly: worn tyres dramatically reduce grip
Responding to a Skid If it happens

If a skid occurs despite prevention:

  • Release the accelerator immediately and smoothly — sudden changes make it worse
  • For a rear skid (oversteer): steer gently in the direction the rear is sliding — "steer into the skid" — without overcorrecting
  • For a front skid (understeer): release the brakes slightly to restore steering grip, then re-apply more gently
  • Never brake hard while skidding: this makes things worse in most cases
  • ABS-equipped vehicles: maintain firm, continuous brake pressure — ABS manages the wheel lock automatically; do not pump the brakes
ABS — Anti-lock Braking System

Most modern vehicles are equipped with ABS. When you apply maximum braking force, ABS rapidly pulsates the brakes to prevent wheel lock-up — maintaining steering control. With ABS, you should press the brake pedal firmly and hold it — do not pump it. The pedal will vibrate and make noise; this is normal. The vehicle will stop in a shorter distance than a locked-wheel skid, while still allowing you to steer around an obstacle.

Fatigue & Attention

Why tiredness is as dangerous as alcohol — and the warning signs that demand you stop.

Fatigue Impairs Like Alcohol Deadly combination

Research consistently shows that being awake for 17 hours produces an impairment equivalent to a blood alcohol level of approximately 0.5 ‰ — the Dutch legal limit. After 24 hours without sleep, the impairment is equivalent to 1.0 ‰ — twice the legal limit.

Unlike alcohol, fatigue has no breathalyser test. But it affects reaction time, judgement, lane-keeping and hazard perception in exactly the same ways. Drivers who fall asleep at the wheel cause high-speed accidents with no braking at all.

Warning Signs of Dangerous Fatigue Act immediately

These warning signs indicate you must stop driving as soon as safely possible:

  • Difficulty keeping your eyes open or head upright
  • Missing road signs or junctions you intended to take
  • Drifting across lanes without intending to
  • Involuntary "microsleeps" — brief moments of unconsciousness lasting 1–3 seconds
  • Inability to remember the last few kilometres you drove
  • Yawning repeatedly and continuously
  • Restlessness and irritability without apparent cause
When any of these warning signs appear, open the window and turn on music are not solutions — they delay the inevitable by only a few minutes. The only effective response is to stop and sleep.
Managing Fatigue on Long Journeys Prevention

For long journeys, plan your fatigue management before you leave:

  • Do not drive more than two hours without a break — take a break of at least 15–20 minutes
  • Do not start a long journey already tired — sleep well the night before
  • Avoid long journeys between midnight and 6:00 AM — natural circadian rhythm causes maximum sleepiness during these hours
  • A short nap of 15–20 minutes at a motorway service area, combined with a coffee, is the most effective short-term fatigue remedy
  • If travelling with a passenger, share driving or take turns resting

Vehicle Condition

Your legal obligation to keep your vehicle roadworthy — and what to check.

The Owner's Duty Roadworthiness

The driver — and the vehicle owner — are legally responsible for ensuring that the vehicle is in a safe and roadworthy condition before it is driven on public roads. Driving a vehicle with known defects is a violation of both the RVV 1990 and the Wegenverkeerswet. If a defect causes an accident, the driver faces both criminal and civil liability.

🔵 Tyres

Minimum tread depth of 1.6 mm across the central 75% of the tyre width and around the full circumference. Tyres below this are illegal. Check tyre pressure regularly — under-inflated tyres increase braking distance and fuel consumption; over-inflated tyres reduce grip.

🔴 Brakes

Brakes must be effective and consistent. Signs of brake problems: squealing, grinding, pulling to one side when braking, soft or spongy pedal, or vibration through the pedal. Any of these require immediate inspection.

💡 Lights

All lights must function: headlights, rear lights, brake lights, indicators, reversing lights. A non-functioning brake light is an immediate safety hazard — following drivers cannot see you braking. Check lights regularly, especially before winter when they are used more.

🔧 Steering

Steering should feel direct and consistent. Excessive play in the steering wheel, pulling to one side, or vibration through the wheel indicates a problem requiring inspection. Tyre imbalance also causes steering vibration at certain speeds.

🪟 Windows & mirrors

Windscreen must be clear — no cracks in the driver's line of sight. All mirrors must be present, intact and correctly adjusted before driving. Defrosting and demisting must be complete before moving — driving with obscured vision is illegal.

📋 APK (MOT equivalent)

Dutch vehicles must pass a periodic roadworthiness test — the APK (Algemene Periodieke Keuring). Frequency depends on vehicle age: new cars first APK after 4 years, then every 2 years. Driving without a valid APK is a violation. An APK sticker in the windscreen shows the expiry date.

BLOWFISH — A Simple Daily Check Routine

A useful memory tool for a quick pre-drive vehicle check: Brakes, Lights, Oil, Water (coolant), Fuel, Indicators, Steering, Hornl. A 60-second check before a long journey can identify obvious problems before they become emergencies on the road.

How road surface, weather and environmental conditions affect safe driving speed and behaviour.

Aquaplaning — What It Is and What to Do Loss of control

Aquaplaning (also called hydroplaning) occurs when a vehicle is travelling fast enough on a wet road that the tyres cannot displace the water quickly enough. The tyre rises up on a film of water and loses all contact with the road surface — steering and braking become temporarily useless.

Signs of aquaplaning: the steering suddenly becomes very light, engine revs may rise, the vehicle drifts in a straight line regardless of steering input.

What to do: ease off the accelerator smoothly — do not brake, do not steer sharply. Allow the vehicle to slow naturally until the tyres regain contact. Then steer gently back to your lane.

The risk of aquaplaning increases with speed and decreases with tyre tread depth. At 80 km/h, a tyre with adequate tread displaces about 15 litres of water per second. At the legal minimum tread depth of 1.6 mm, this capacity is dramatically reduced.
Winter Driving Snow & Ice

The Netherlands does not legally mandate winter tyres — but under conditions of snow and ice, winter tyres reduce stopping distances by up to 50% compared to summer tyres. The responsible driver fits winter tyres when conditions require them.

Before driving in winter conditions:

  • Remove all snow from the vehicle — roof, bonnet, windows, lights — before driving. Snow flying off your vehicle onto following drivers is a violation
  • Allow full demisting before moving — do not drive with a porthole-sized clear patch
  • Check tyre pressure — cold weather reduces pressure
  • Allow significantly more time for journeys
  • Carry a blanket, emergency food and phone charger for breakdowns in cold conditions
Supplement B — What to Take Away

Stopping distance = reaction distance + braking distance. Braking distance increases with the square of speed. Maintain a minimum two-second following distance — more in adverse conditions. Your speed must always allow you to stop within your sight line. Fatigue is as dangerous as alcohol — the only cure is sleep. Tyres must have a minimum 1.6 mm tread depth. Aquaplaning: ease off the accelerator, do not brake or steer until grip returns.
